headline: AI measurements of heart scans predicted survival slightly better than doctors' measurements, in seconds
what_happened: Researchers at City St George's, University of London and University College London compared an AI tool with experienced clinicians at measuring how well the heart pumps from MRI scans of 27,382 patients in the UK and the United States. Most scans came from Barts Heart Centre in London, and 3,458 patients died over a median follow-up of 5.6 years. The AI's measurements were slightly but significantly better at predicting who died, and the study was published in The Lancet Digital Health on 2 November 2026.
why_its_good: The AI did in about 2 to 3 seconds per patient a measurement that takes an expert around 13 minutes, and its numbers were at least as good a guide to survival. The researchers support using it as a first check on heart MRI scans, with experts reviewing where needed.
careful: The gain is small: a C index of 0.781 for the AI against 0.777 for clinicians
It looked back at old scans, so it shows a link with survival, not that using the tool helps patients live longer
The tool is not described as being in routine use
The 2 to 3 seconds against 13 minutes figure comes from the team's earlier work, not from this study
The senior author invented the tool
About 1% of patients had an AI error, so clinicians still need to check

headline: Breast cancer patients in Croatia understood AI-written research summaries as well as the originals
what_happened: Researchers at the University Hospital of Split in Croatia gave 133 women with breast cancer that had not spread a plain-language summary of two Cochrane research reviews, one on exercise during treatment and one on psychological support. Half read the original summaries and half read versions written in Croatian by ChatGPT-4o, and neither patients nor researchers knew which was which. There was no overall difference in how well the women understood the summaries, how much they trusted them, how clear they found them or whether they intended to act on them. The study was published in Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence on 16 November 2026.
why_its_good: The AI produced patient summaries that real patients found as clear and trustworthy as ones written by people, which points to a quicker way of putting medical evidence into plain words for patients. The authors say expert checking is still needed before such summaries reach patients.
careful: The finding is 'no overall difference', not that the AI summaries were better.
Answers were collected straight after reading; the study did not measure whether anyone changed behaviour or had better health.

what_happened: Han Won-seok, the top scorer in South Korea's 63rd certified tax accountant exam, said on a lawyer's YouTube channel that he photographed the questions with a miniature camera, sent them to an AI and read the answers on a smartphone, and he reported himself to the police. On Sunday 15 November the presidential policy chief and the vice minister of employment and labour each chaired an emergency meeting. The authorities said they will examine every national licensing exam held this year for AI cheating, open tip-off centres and deliver an anti-cheating plan by the end of the year, and the exam agency apologised and decided to file a complaint against him.
why_its_good: The cheating came to light because the person responsible owned up, and within days the government and the exam agency were acting on it across all national licensing exams. Honest candidates are the ones who gain from that.
bad_news: The top scorer in a South Korean national tax accountant exam cheated in both rounds using a hidden camera, a smartphone and generative AI, sitting in front of two proctors who did not notice, and the exam agency's own review had found nothing wrong.
careful: Radio-wave detectors are not in use. One report says they are being developed and will be deployed quickly, another says they are only under review and will not be considered until next year. Do not say they are being rolled out.
The review of all exams, the tip-off centres and the year-end plan are announced measures, not finished ones.
Penalties (results cancelled, five-year ban, criminal referral) are described as being pursued or under consideration, not imposed.
The exam agency did not catch the cheating; on 13 November it had said it found no irregularities. Do not credit the system with detecting it.
The sources opened do not report any cheating in the college entrance exam (CSAT); the tighter CSAT rules are a precaution.
Han did not disclose his exact method. The Kyunghyang article refers to him only as 'A'; his name comes from the Korea Herald.
Do not suggest the AI or the cheating was clever or impressive, and do not play down that a professional licence was obtained by cheating.
The story is little known outside South Korea, which weakens it as a flip for UK readers.

headline: South Korea bans AI glasses from its university entrance exam and promises checks at every test site
what_happened: South Korea's education ministry added AI glasses to the list of items banned at the national university entrance exam in July 2026 and issued guidelines for handling cheating cases. On 29 October it said it would assign one inspector to each test site to check for the glasses, starting with this year's exam on 19 November, and would seek criminal prosecution of anyone caught. On 13 November the Office for Government Policy Coordination promised zero tolerance, said specialist staff would be sent to test sites, and said it would ask for an investigation into suspected cheating in this year's tax accountant exam.
why_its_good: The authorities moved before the country's biggest exam, not after it, with a ban already in force and named checks at test sites. Students sitting the exam honestly are the ones who benefit.
bad_news: People in South Korea have been caught or suspected of using AI glasses and other AI tools to cheat in exams, including university entrance exams, and the top score in this year's tax accountant exam (397.5 out of 400) is under suspicion.
careful: Nobody has been caught cheating at the national entrance exam (CSAT) itself; it takes place on 19 November 2026, after these announcements. The cheating cases are from other exams.
The inspectors and specialist staff are announced plans for the 19 November exam; the sources do not show them at work yet.
The three-year exam ban is something the ministry is pushing for, not yet the rule; the current exclusion is one year.
Radio wave detectors are only under review for next year's exam.
Cheating in the tax accountant exam is suspected, not confirmed, in the article opened.
Do not mention the LEET law school test case or any police investigation of an individual; no source for those was opened.
The sources do not say how many cheating cases there have been.
